title: Ten Things to Know about the RITE Method (MeasuringU)
label: practitioner
claim: RITE (Medlock et al. 2002, Age of Empires II): fix a problem as soon as one participant reveals it, then keep testing. AoE II: 10 participants with fixes, then 6 with no changes as verification. Stopping-rule maths: after 1 change-free participant you have only found problems hitting >=80%; after 6, ~25%. Needs fixes that take under an hour or two. No study has compared RITE with ordinary rapid formative testing; many teams skip the verification step.

title: Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users (Nielsen)
label: research
claim: Problems found = N(1-(1-L)^n), L about 31%. Claim holds only with iteration (3 rounds of 5 beat 1 of 15) and comparable users; test 3-4 per distinct user group, never fewer than 3.

title: Enough is enough (Human Factors newsletter, summarising Spool & Schroeder 2001, Perfetti & Landesman 2002, Virzi)
label: research
claim: Critics: first five users found about 35% of problems of a larger set (Spool & Schroeder); participants 6-18 each found 5+ problems missed by the first five (Perfetti & Landesman); Virzi's own 5-user sample found anywhere from 55% to ~100%. Web-site studies, not games.

title: Kolibri Games / PlaytestCloud case study, Idle Miner Tycoon
label: developer
claim: 7 remote players, three 15-minute sessions with 2-hour gaps, to mirror idle play. Found players stalled before a retention-linked milestone because they upgraded mines but ignored elevators/warehouses (resources piled up). Fix: contextual tutorials; more reached the milestone, churn and negative reviews fell. Vendor-published, outcome figures not given.

title: PlaytestCloud: methods for playtesting
label: practitioner
claim: Separates usability testing (few players, intensive per-player analysis, remote or in person, moderated or not) from appreciation/fun testing (larger samples, surveys, diary and multi-session studies); warns that mixing both goals in one study gets complicated. Challenge is intended in games, so task speed is not the measure.

title: How first session length impacts game performance (deltaDNA, Game Developer 2016)
label: research
claim: 275 'comparable' games, Oct 2015-Feb 2016: first sessions over the 9-minute mean had 31% D1 retention vs 20%. Author admits short sessions may be an effect of churn, not a cause; selection of the 275 not explained.

title: Expert tips for writing a playtest survey (Games User Research)
label: practitioner
claim: Pilot every survey as a qualitative test; one idea per question; give a 'never' option; completion drops after ~5 minutes and past 10 minutes only a biased subset finish; players use different words from the team, so end with a broad open question; make it phone-friendly.

title: Valve biofeedback slides (Ambinder, GDC 2011)
label: developer
claim: Valve's own slide: aim of physiological measures is 'more objective responses': 'Lots of biases in current playtesting procedures'; pairs sensor data with survey responses (enjoyment, frustration) and timestamped game events. The 2009 Valve playtesting talk itself was not retrievable.

title: Valve biofeedback talk page / PC Gamer coverage
label: snippet
claim: Valve tested an arousal-driven Left 4 Dead 2 director; post-play surveys rated it about twice as enjoyable (reported by PC Gamer, not seen first-hand).

title: Pagulayan, Steury, Fulton, Romero: Designing for Fun, user-testing case studies (Funology, 2003)
label: research
claim: Microsoft Games User Research chapter on user testing in games; full text not retrievable (gamestudies.org copy refused connection).

title: Student playtest reflection on curse of knowledge
label: opinion
claim: Single anecdote: the playtest where the designer said nothing gave the clearest picture; confusion cleared faster. Designers cannot imagine not knowing what they know.

title: Bugnet playtest guides (several)
label: practitioner
claim: Stay silent, watch hesitation and stuck points; explaining mid-test hands the tester information the shipped game won't; observer effect changes how daring testers are; players cannot always say why they feel something and propose fixes from a flawed model. Unsourced advice, widely repeated.

title: Valve playtesting slides (Ambinder, GDC 2009)
label: developer
claim: Valve's own method table. Direct observation: '+ importance of what people do, not what they say'; '- presence of observers can bias results; salient event can slant interpretation; behavior requires interpretation'. Think-aloud (unprompted, uncorrected, with observation): '+ effective for why questions; - interferes with gameplay, inaccurate and biased'. Q&A: '- people don't know why they do what they do; group biases'. 'Nothing beats direct gameplay observation.' Philosophy: game designs are hypotheses, playtests experiments; get data early, iterate constantly; playtest goal is fun, not bug testing or balancing. Stats: 'averages hide extreme examples; can see illusory patterns'.

title: Medlock, Wixon, Terrano, Romero, Fulton: Using the RITE method to improve products (UPA 2002)
label: research
claim: Primary paper. Fix when problem and solution are clear, sometimes after 1 participant; think-aloud used. Preconditions: agreed must-pass tasks before test; changes in under 2 hours or by next test day; decision makers present; experienced usability engineer. Issues sorted into 4 categories; unclear-cause issues get more participants before any fix. AoE II tutorial: 16 participants (5F, 11M, none had played RTS), changes between participants 1,2,5,8,9,10, then 6 more with no regression; 88% likely all fixes worked at p=0.30, 47% at p=0.10 (Lewis binomial tables). 31 problems found, 30 fixed; 6 of 36 fixes needed re-fixing (20%); 'train' vs 'create' unit wording failed once, 6 of 8 testers stuck before the re-fix. Spikes after a fix because testers get further.

title: Hodent at DigiPen (news report of talk)
label: developer
claim: Hodent: 'You know your design, so it's really hard to have objective knowledge of it, because you can't step back' (curse of knowledge); remedy: 'bring people in who are your target audience and see how people actually interact with the game'; UX 'the earlier the better'. Secondhand report, not her own text.

title: Games User Research Methods (Bromley)
label: practitioner
claim: Think-aloud: 'an unnatural task, introduces some cognitive load'; 'may lead people to the right answer'; works best in co-op games where players explain to each other. Observation: researchers 'will find it difficult to reliably observe more than one or two participants at a time'; paired with probing questions; suits 'do players learn the objectives'.

title: Running a games user research study (Bromley)
label: practitioner
claim: Moderator 'cannot just sit in silence' but must stay neutral, not confirm or dismiss opinions, not introduce new ideas. Does not address developers watching sessions.

title: Valve's Faliszek: Playtesters aren't idiots, it's you
label: developer
claim: Valve's early reaction to outside testers was to blame them; by the third or fourth round the team accepted 'it's our fault'. 'Playtesting is just proof to you.'

title: The Playtests that Changed 2XKO (Riot)
label: developer
claim: Riot runs many playtests with mixed groups (devs, new-to-genre players, high-skill communities) combining observation, designer intent and raw numbers; says feedback is weighed for whether a change fixes the cause or only the symptom. No method detail on onboarding.

title: Spool & Schroeder 2001 CHI abstract: five users is nowhere near enough
label: snippet
claim: Abstract only via search snippet: 49 users, same task, four production web sites. A secondary page (syntagm.co.uk) instead says 18 users and goal-directed buy-something tasks; conflict unresolved. Full text not retrievable (acm 403, academia 403).
